row.basis: Evening and morning form one day
row.note: The commentary joins night to day as parts of time; Genesis names light day and darkness night, then closes the first day with evening and morning, giving the pair an ordered whole.

row.basis: Day/night and winter/summer succession
row.note: The commentary links successive days with winter's appointed interval; the promise that seedtime, harvest, cold, heat, summer, winter, day, and night will not cease makes those alternating parts a stable covenantal rhythm.

row.basis: Day speaks to day, night to night
row.note: The commentary pictures adjoining periods as a chain; the psalm has each day pour speech into the next and each night disclose knowledge to the next, making succession itself communicative.

row.basis: Day and night belong to God
row.note: The commentary treats the paired periods as more than an undifferentiated flow; the psalm addresses God as owner of both day and night and maker of the luminaries that mark them.

row.basis: Summer and winter formed by God
row.note: The commentary moves from daily pairs to winter's middle and cold; this verse attributes the formation of summer and winter, as well as earth's bounds, to God.

row.basis: An appointed time for every affair
row.note: The commentary calls time a sequence of distinct intervals; Ecclesiastes introduces its paired occasions by assigning each affair its own time under heaven.

row.basis: Birth and death have their times
row.note: The commentary develops youth, age, and the end of life; this pair places birth and death at separate appointed moments rather than treating a life as a single span.

row.basis: A thousand years like yesterday
row.note: The commentary says a long lifetime shrinks to an evening or a daytime hour when viewed at the end; the psalm compares a thousand years before God to yesterday once passed and to a night watch.

row.basis: Humans are of yesterday
row.note: The commentary puts human life inside a vast time before one existed; Bildad says humans are only of yesterday and know little because their earthly days are a shadow.

row.basis: Number days to gain wisdom
row.note: The commentary makes the countable stages of a life matter for righteous action; the psalm asks God to teach humans to count their days so that they acquire a wise heart.

row.basis: My times are in your hand
row.note: The commentary places the pieces and limits of a person's life under God's ordering; the psalmist entrusts his own times to God's hand while asking deliverance from enemies.

row.basis: Days written before any existed
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes a long time before human existence with life's later stages; the psalm says the speaker's days were recorded when none of them had yet come, placing the life course in divine foreknowledge.

row.basis: Remember the creator in youth
row.note: The commentary names youth as one interval of a finite life; Ecclesiastes commands remembrance specifically in youthful days before difficult later years arrive.

row.basis: Old age and the next generation
row.note: The commentary joins successive life stages to people sustaining one another; the aged speaker asks not to be forsaken until he tells the next generation of God's power.

row.basis: Even a century is a small life span
row.note: The commentary counts human ages and then reduces a whole life to a brief interval; Sirach calls a hundred years a large number of human days before measuring them against eternity.

row.basis: Few years beside eternal days
row.note: The commentary says lengthy human residence looks like only a small daytime fraction; Sirach likens human years against eternity to a drop of sea water or a grain of sand.

row.basis: The impious claim death returns them to nonexistence
row.note: The commentary recalls the claim that time alone destroys and counters it with final reckoning; Wisdom puts in the impious speakers' mouths the claim that chance brought them into being and afterward they will be as though they had never existed.

row.basis: Life as a passing shadow
row.note: The commentary says the long stay contracts to an evening or an hour; the impious speakers in Wisdom compare life to a passing shadow, though the book presents their conclusion about death as mistaken.

row.basis: Truth taught while waiting all day
row.note: The commentary places counsel in truth and patience inside the day's span; the psalmist asks to be taught God's truth and says he waits for God all day.

row.basis: Appointed vision, waiting through delay
row.note: The commentary binds patience to a true promise whose fulfillment has its own time; the vision points to its appointed end and the hearer must wait even if it seems delayed.

row.basis: Blessed one who waits through counted days
row.note: The commentary makes endurance stretch over a measured interval; Daniel blesses the person who waits to the specified day count, joining a finite duration to perseverance.

row.basis: Torah meditated day and night
row.note: The commentary sets truth-oriented persistence across the two periods; the righteous person's meditation on the Torah fills both day and night.

row.basis: Day-night instruction becomes action
row.note: The commentary joins right deeds to a time-spanning attachment to truth; Joshua must meditate on the book of Torah day and night so that he acts according to it.

row.basis: Teach others at lying down and rising
row.note: The commentary says people become linked through repeated counsel while time passes; Israel is to teach the words to children while sitting, walking, lying down, and rising.

row.basis: Morning instruction sustains the weary
row.note: The commentary has people uphold one another through truth across successive mornings; the servant receives an awakened ear morning by morning so he can sustain the weary with a word.

row.basis: The God-fearing speak to one another
row.note: The commentary depicts the surviving group as people bound by reciprocal exhortation; those who fear God speak together, and God attends to them and records their remembrance.

row.basis: Speak truth to one's neighbor
row.note: The commentary's mutual counsel is specifically counsel in truth; Zechariah commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor and to render truthful, peace-making judgments.

row.basis: One group urges another to seek God
row.note: The commentary's people attach themselves to one another through counsel; the city's inhabitants invite others to go entreat God and add that they themselves will go.

row.basis: Accumulation and ignorance of its heir
row.note: The commentary recalls the preceding surah's race to multiply possessions until death; the psalm says a person heaps wealth without knowing who will gather it after him. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, but this row rests on the developed accumulation motif, not a claimed shared meaning with patience.

row.basis: Winter labor and later want
row.note: The commentary gives winter's cold a place in patient seasonal time; the sluggard refuses to plow in winter and therefore seeks food at harvest without finding it, showing how one interval governs the next.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: fixed life limit
row.note: The table offers a sound correspondence only, not proven cognacy; Job says a human's days and months are determined and God set a חק, a limit he cannot pass, a specific counterpart to the commentary's allotted life stages and due times.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: prescribed light cycles
row.note: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; Jeremiah calls the sun for daylight and the moon and stars for night divinely established ordinances, connecting the commentary's linked periods to a prescribed cosmic order.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: enduring ordinances
row.note: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; the continued existence of Israel is made contingent on those day-night ordinances departing, linking regular time to the survival of a people.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: inscribed light-dark boundary
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Job describes a marked circle on the waters at the boundary of light and darkness, giving the commentary's adjoining night and day a sharply marked boundary.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: eighth-day assembly
row.note: The table gives a sound correspondence, not a proven cognate of time; after seven days of offerings this verse prescribes an eighth-day עצרת, where successive counted days culminate in people assembling.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: seventh-day assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence alone does not establish cognacy; after six days of unleavened bread the seventh is an עצרת, joining a counted sequence to communal gathering as in the commentary's meeting of time and people.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: daily reading, eighth-day assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Ezra reads the Torah day by day through the festival, then the people hold an eighth-day עצרת, making repeated instruction and a final joined assembly one timed practice.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: call an assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; the command to blow the trumpet, sanctify a fast, and call an עצרה gives the commentary's people joined through urgent exhortation a concrete communal form.

row.basis: Every age gathers together
row.note: The commentary names stages of life before showing people joined; Joel's summoned gathering explicitly includes elders, children, nursing infants, bridegroom, and bride.

row.basis: Assembly joined to injustice is rejected
row.note: The commentary makes righteous deeds and truth conditions of collective survival; Isaiah refuses an assembly held together with wrongdoing, testing the value of a gathered religious community by its conduct. Hebrew עצרה is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r, without proof of cognacy.

row.basis: Endurance until the end
row.note: The commentary says those who endure remain through the chain of time; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, making persistence across the whole interval decisive.

row.basis: Stored years collapse into one night
row.note: The commentary contrasts a lifetime of numerical accumulation with its abrupt end; the rich man's planned many years are cut short that very night, and he is asked who will have his stored goods.

row.basis: Possessions imagined to guarantee many years
row.note: The commentary links the competition to increase possessions with failure to notice time passing; the rich man addresses his soul as though stored goods secured many years of rest.

row.basis: Enlarged barns for accumulated goods
row.note: The commentary recalls multiplying wealth until the grave; the rich man decides to build larger barns to store all his grain and goods before his mortality is exposed in the story.

row.basis: Life appears briefly and vanishes
row.note: The commentary reduces a seeming long residence to a small interval; James calls human life a vapor that appears a little while and disappears, addressing people who plan future years.

row.basis: One day and a thousand years
row.note: The commentary contrasts long duration with its apparent contraction; this verse reversibly compares one day and a thousand years before the Lord, relativizing ordinary measures of waiting.

row.basis: Delayed promise and divine patience
row.note: The commentary connects patience to the true promise through a shrinking lifetime; this verse says the promised coming is not slow as some reckon but delayed in divine patience to allow repentance.

row.basis: Appointed periods for human peoples
row.note: The commentary divides time into assigned intervals while people remain joined; Paul says God made every nation from one and determined their appointed times and dwelling boundaries.

row.basis: The remaining time is shortened
row.note: The commentary says a long life is seen as compressed when its end approaches; Paul tells believers the appointed time has grown short and therefore their ordinary life relations must be held lightly.

row.basis: Outer decline, daily inner renewal
row.note: The commentary tracks bodily life through aging while patience persists across days; Paul says the outer person wastes away but the inner person is renewed day by day.

row.basis: Exhort one another every day
row.note: The commentary's people remain joined through reciprocal counsel across linked days; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation while it is called Today, to prevent hardening through sin.

row.basis: Stir one another to good works
row.note: The commentary makes shared righteous action part of how people remain connected; Hebrews asks believers to consider one another so as to provoke love and good deeds.

row.basis: Gather and encourage as the Day approaches
row.note: The commentary connects communal exhortation to passing time; Hebrews opposes abandoning assembly and urges increasingly mutual encouragement as the approaching Day is seen.

row.basis: Three years of night-and-day admonition
row.note: The commentary ties mutual counsel to morning/evening and a lasting interval; Paul recalls three years in which he warned each person night and day with tears.

row.basis: Exhort at every season with patience
row.note: The commentary's counsel and patience fill successive times; the charge to proclaim the word in season and out of season includes correction and exhortation with complete patience and teaching.

row.basis: Good action sustained until its season
row.note: The commentary joins righteous deeds and patience across time; Paul says not to grow weary in doing good because a harvest will come at its proper time if people do not give up.

row.basis: Night is advanced, day draws near
row.note: The commentary makes night-to-day transition a call to moral action; Paul says the passing night and approaching day demand casting off dark works and taking up the armor of light.

row.basis: Work during the remaining day
row.note: The commentary links right deeds to the short allotted interval; Jesus says the works of the sender must be done while it is day, since night comes when no one can work.

row.basis: Use the time because days are evil
row.note: The commentary makes limited time the setting for righteous action; Ephesians asks its hearers to make the most of the time because the days are evil.

row.basis: Elect cry day and night for justice
row.note: The commentary places truth and patient appeal across daily cycles; Jesus describes God's chosen crying to him day and night for justice in a parable about persistent prayer.

row.basis: The slain ask how long until judgment
row.note: The commentary connects waiting with a true final reckoning; the slain ask the sovereign Lord how long before he judges and vindicates their blood.

row.basis: Rest a little longer until number complete
row.note: The commentary gives patient waiting a finite interval and links the fates of people; the martyrs are told to rest a little longer until their fellow servants are complete.

row.basis: Endurance, divine commands, and faith
row.note: The commentary's surviving group combines belief, deeds, and patience; Revelation characterizes the saints' endurance by keeping God's commandments and faith in Jesus.

row.basis: Speaking truth together builds maturity
row.note: The commentary makes counsel in truth a way people are joined; speaking truth in love is the means by which members grow toward their common head, Christ.

row.basis: The body joined by every working part
row.note: The commentary says the people who remain are added to one another; the body is joined and held together as each part works, building itself up in love.

row.basis: Encourage and build one another
row.note: The commentary's repeated reciprocal counsel makes a durable community; Paul explicitly tells believers to encourage one another and build one another up.

row.basis: Admonish, help, and be patient with all
row.note: The commentary couples mutual counsel with patience; this instruction names admonishing the idle, helping the weak, and being patient with everyone as communal practices.

row.basis: Winter intensifies the coming ordeal
row.note: The commentary names winter's hard cold as one temporal condition for patience; Jesus tells hearers to pray that their flight does not occur in winter, when that season will worsen their urgent journey.

row.basis: Morning mercy and nightly faithfulness
row.note: The commentary pairs morning and evening as recurring occasions for patient devotion; the sabbath psalm assigns proclamation of God's kindness to morning and his faithfulness to nights.

row.basis: Remember God at night and keep law
row.note: The commentary has enduring adherence to truth through the nighttime portion; the psalmist remembers God's name at night and keeps his law.

row.basis: Wake through night watches for instruction
row.note: The commentary makes patient fidelity stretch across night and morning; the psalmist's eyes anticipate the watches of the night to meditate on God's saying.

row.basis: Evening, morning, noon prayer
row.note: The commentary explicitly pairs morning with late day; the psalmist names evening, morning, and noon as repeated times of appeal to God, dividing the day into acts of persistence.

row.basis: Daytime care and nighttime song
row.note: The commentary makes night and day adjoining parts of a lived religious interval; the psalmist expects God's kindness by day and a song-prayer with him at night.

row.basis: Human cannot grasp time's whole work
row.note: The commentary says the connected pieces are more than a flat flow; Ecclesiastes says God made each thing fitting in its time while humans cannot discover the work from beginning to end.

row.basis: Old age approaches the lasting home
row.note: The commentary takes youth through decline to the grave; Ecclesiastes' portrait of the aging person's fears ends with going to the lasting home while mourners walk outside.

row.basis: Seventy or eighty years pass quickly
row.note: The commentary catalogs life stages but says all that time can contract at the end; the psalm gives a human span of seventy or eighty years and says it quickly passes.

row.basis: Infant and elder days transformed
row.note: The commentary counts childhood and old age among life's parts; Isaiah's promised city reverses premature death, saying infants will not live only a few days and elders will complete their days.

row.basis: As though never existing, womb to grave
row.note: The commentary recalls a time when a human was not yet a mentioned thing and a later journey to death; Job wishes he had been as though he had not existed, carried directly from womb to grave.

row.basis: Days as a passing shadow
row.note: The commentary compresses lifetime into a brief seeming stay; the psalm says human days resemble a shadow that passes away.

row.basis: Human lifetime as grass
row.note: The commentary's phases of life culminate in disappearance; the psalm compares mortal days to grass flourishing briefly as a flower of the field.

row.basis: A passing wind erases its place
row.note: The commentary asks how much of a long life remains at its end; when wind passes over the flower it is gone and its place knows it no more, the next part of the mortal image.

row.basis: Winter has passed
row.note: The commentary calls winter a particular hard interval and ties waiting to its end; the lover announces that winter and its rain are over, so the harsh season has a bounded duration.

row.basis: Ant stores food in summer and harvest
row.note: The commentary connects accumulation to passing time; the ant gathers provisions in summer and at harvest, supplying a purposeful seasonal counterpart to accumulation that distracts humans until death.

row.basis: Wicked person piles silver
row.note: The commentary recalls competitive increase of possessions before mortality; Job's wicked figure heaps silver like dust and clothing like clay, preparing the reversal in the next verse. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, not a demonstrated shared sense with patience.

row.basis: Another receives what was piled
row.note: The commentary's hoarder cannot carry accumulated time or goods beyond life's end; Job says the righteous will wear the wicked person's prepared clothes and the innocent will divide his silver.

row.basis: Joseph heaps grain across good years
row.note: The commentary recalls multiplying material stores before a later interval; Joseph piles grain beyond counting ahead of famine, giving accumulation a collective preserving purpose. Hebrew צבר is only the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r; the connection is the concrete stored-grain scene.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: day-night statutes
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God's fixed ordinances of heaven and earth accompany his covenant with day and night, tying the commentary's alternating periods to continuing communal existence.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: heaven's ordinances
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God asks Job whether he knows the ordinances of heaven or can establish their rule on earth, an interpretive bridge from the commentary's due times to cosmic prescription.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: assigned sea boundary
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; Wisdom recalls God setting the sea its prescribed limit, a spatial analogue to the commentary's precisely bounded intervals and seasonal middles.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: communal crisis assembly
row.note: The table's sound correspondence does not prove cognacy; Joel calls a fast and an עצרה in which elders and all inhabitants gather at God's house and cry out, linking group survival to shared action in a hard time.

row.basis: Be still and wait despite evildoer success
row.note: The commentary says patience must be sustained while truth is not yet manifest; the psalm tells its hearer to wait patiently for God rather than fret over a person succeeding in an evil course.

row.basis: Waiting renews strength
row.note: The commentary treats patience as what lets people keep standing through a long interval; Isaiah says those waiting for God renew strength and continue without fainting.

row.basis: Quietly wait for salvation
row.note: The commentary connects a difficult period with patient endurance; Lamentations calls quiet waiting for God's salvation good amid its account of suffering.

row.basis: Three daily prayers despite hostile decree
row.note: The commentary stretches the act of patience between recurring times of day; Daniel continues praying three times daily even after the written decree against that practice.

row.basis: People hold onto another to go together
row.note: The commentary says people are added to one another through a shared orientation to God; Zechariah imagines people of many languages grasping a Jew's garment and asking to go with him because God is with the group.

row.basis: One person sharpens another
row.note: The commentary's reciprocal exhortation makes persons sustain one another; the proverb compares one person's effect on a friend to iron sharpening iron, giving counsel a mutual formative action.

row.basis: Named ages of a human life
row.note: The commentary explicitly parses youth, maturity, and decline as time's pieces; Avot gives a sequence of ages with different pursuits and capacities, including forty for understanding and seventy for old age. Section numbering varies by edition.

row.basis: Acquire a friend and a teacher
row.note: The commentary makes people remain linked by guidance; Avot directs a person to make a teacher and acquire a friend, turning endurance into a sustained interpersonal practice.

row.basis: If not now, when; if only for self, what am I
row.note: The commentary binds short time to the need for others; Hillel's paired questions reject delay and self-enclosure in the same ethical saying.

row.basis: Do not defer study until free time
row.note: The commentary says time is spent in successive limited pieces; Avot warns that a hoped-for leisure interval may never come, making present instruction urgent.

row.basis: Repent one day before death
row.note: The commentary says a long life can shrink suddenly to its last fraction; the rabbinic explanation of repentance one day before death is to repent each day because no one knows which day will be last.

row.basis: Evening before morning in prayer order
row.note: The commentary puts night and day into a deliberate sequence; the discussion explains beginning the daily Shema with evening by appealing to creation's evening followed by morning, turning Genesis' order into a repeated act.

row.basis: Prayer and fasting night and day
row.note: The commentary places steadfast worship across the paired periods; the aged Anna serves in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day, joining old age with continuous devotion.

row.basis: Hope for unseen end requires patience
row.note: The commentary asks people to wait through an interval for a promised resolution; Paul says those hoping for what they do not yet see wait for it with endurance.

row.basis: Endurance receives the promised thing
row.note: The commentary joins patience to the true promise; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will so that hearers may receive what was promised.

row.basis: Divine patience counted as salvation
row.note: The commentary joins the waiting interval to the chance to remain among the saved; Peter explicitly asks readers to regard the Lord's patience as salvation, supplying the purpose of the delay.

row.basis: Farmer waits through seasonal rains
row.note: The commentary names winter's severity and the waiting that spans seasons; James asks believers to be patient like a farmer waiting for precious fruit through early and late rain until the Lord's coming.

row.basis: Prophets as examples of patient speech
row.note: The commentary couples truth-telling with endurance; James names prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.

row.basis: Present opportunity used for good to all
row.note: The commentary says righteous deeds and mutual support occupy limited time; Paul says that while opportunity remains believers should do good to everyone, especially fellow believers.

row.basis: Teach and admonish one another
row.note: The commentary defines the surviving group through mutual counsel; Colossians asks believers to let Christ's word dwell among them as they teach and admonish one another wisely.

row.basis: Speak truth as members of one another
row.note: The commentary brings truth and people being joined into one image; Ephesians gives membership in one body as the reason for each person to speak truth to a neighbor.

row.basis: Patient affliction with persistent prayer
row.note: The commentary stretches patience between repeated times of worship; Paul joins patience in tribulation to constancy in prayer as the group's practice.

row.basis: Day of the Lord arrives during night
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes the day-night pair with the sudden end of a seeming long stay; Paul says the Lord's day comes like a thief in the night, challenging complacency about the remaining time.

row.basis: Believers belong to day, not night
row.note: The commentary makes remaining people a distinct group amid the alternation of night and day; Paul calls believers children of light and day, assigning the temporal images an ethical identity.

row.basis: Wakefulness instead of sleep
row.note: The commentary develops short sleep and patient alertness across time; Paul tells the community not to sleep as others do but to keep awake and sober in view of the approaching day.

row.basis: Rich are to become rich in good works
row.note: The commentary contrasts accumulating possessions with righteous action that endures; Paul instructs the rich to be rich in good works and generous to others.

row.basis: Store a foundation for the future life
row.note: The commentary's accumulation motif ends at the grave unless joined to right deeds; Paul pictures generosity as storing a firm foundation for the future so that people may grasp true life.

row.basis: The rich fade in the midst of pursuits
row.note: The commentary says acquisitive effort can consume the person's unnoticed time; James likens a rich person's fading during pursuits to a flower withered by the rising sun.

row.basis: Twelve hours mark the usable day
row.note: The commentary treats the day as a bounded segment in which one's way matters; Jesus asks whether the day has twelve hours and connects walking without stumbling to its light.

row.basis: Faithful waiting through night watches
row.note: The commentary puts patience across segmented night; Jesus calls servants blessed if found alert when their master comes in the second or third watch.

row.basis: Pray flight will not be in winter
row.note: The commentary treats winter's cold as a concrete trial inside the calendar; Jesus tells hearers to pray that the expected flight not happen in winter, making season alter the hardship of endurance.

row.basis: Companionship sought before winter
row.note: The commentary links winter's coming with people maintaining one another through time; Paul urges his addressee to come before winter, making the seasonal deadline matter for their meeting.

row.basis: Communal service day and night
row.note: The commentary makes daily alternation part of continuing allegiance; the rescued multitude stands before God's throne and serves him day and night, extending joined devotion beyond mortal time.

row.basis: Separate times for scattering and gathering
row.note: The commentary makes successive pieces of time carry opposing actions and later joins people; Ecclesiastes assigns separate times to scattering stones and gathering them, a concrete temporal analogy rather than an explicit claim about people.

row.basis: Known before formation in the womb
row.note: The commentary recalls a span when the human was not yet a mentioned thing; Jeremiah's prophetic commission says God knew him before forming him in the womb, complicating any inference that pre-birth absence means divine unawareness.

row.basis: Afflicted yet remembers prescribed words
row.note: The commentary makes endurance in truth span harsh conditions; the psalmist describes himself as a wineskin in smoke yet says he has not forgotten God's statutes, though the image is not explicitly winter cold.

row.basis: Tyre piles silver before its fall
row.note: The commentary recalls abundance amassed before a terminal reversal; Tyre heaps silver like dust in this verse before its wealth is stripped in the next. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, with no asserted patience cognacy.

row.basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: withholding birth
row.note: The table gives only a sound correspondence; God asks whether he would bring to birth and then restrain delivery, an indirect counterpart to the commentary's movement through appointed life stages and resistance to time stopping.

row.basis: One not yet born has not seen evil
row.note: The commentary recalls a pre-existence interval in human life; Ecclesiastes calls the unborn person better off because that person has not witnessed oppression, though its judgment about nonexistence has a different purpose.

row.basis: Fathers and young people addressed separately
row.note: The commentary names distinct stages of a life; the letter addresses fathers and young people with different spiritual descriptions, an analogy through communal age categories rather than a literal lifespan sequence.

row.basis: Lights mark days, years, and appointed seasons
row.note: The commentary joins night and day to longer seasonal and lifetime intervals; Genesis assigns the lights the work of marking days, years, and appointed times, making several scales of time depend on the same cycle.

row.basis: Sun returns after setting
row.note: The commentary treats morning and late day as recurring joined pieces; Ecclesiastes has the sun rise, set, and hurry back to the place of its rising.

row.basis: Moon marks appointed times and sun its setting
row.note: The commentary places seasonal middles alongside daily transitions; the psalm says the moon was made for appointed times while the sun knows its setting.

row.basis: Human years swept away like sleep
row.note: The commentary names a short sleep and says a long human span is later perceived as brief; the psalm says God sweeps humans away like sleep before its morning-grass comparison.

row.basis: Morning growth withers by evening
row.note: The commentary compresses a life into the morning-to-evening interval; the psalm's grass flourishes in the morning and fades by evening, completing the time image begun in the preceding verse.

row.basis: Long night spent waiting for dawn
row.note: The commentary develops broken sleep, morning and evening, and patience stretched between them; Job describes lying down, waiting to rise, and tossing through a seemingly prolonged night until dawn.

row.basis: Waiting more than watchmen for morning
row.note: The commentary turns patience into a posture held across night toward morning; the psalmist repeats that his soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for morning.

row.basis: Accumulated wealth cannot go through death
row.note: The commentary recalls multiplying possessions until the grave; the psalm says a wealthy person carries none of it away when dying, specifying the limit that accumulation cannot cross.

row.basis: Riches fail at reckoning, righteousness delivers
row.note: The commentary puts accumulated goods beside righteous deeds and final loss; the proverb says wealth is useless on the day of wrath while righteousness delivers from death.

row.basis: Dust returns but spirit returns to God
row.note: The commentary reports the denial that passing time alone destroys humans and recalls final accountability; Ecclesiastes instead says the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to the God who gave it.

row.basis: The long dead awaken for judgment
row.note: The commentary's brief-seeming stay ends at a gathering where deniers lose; Daniel says many who sleep in the dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to shame, supplying a direct alternative to death as time's final word.

row.basis: Youth faces later judgment
row.note: The commentary names youth as one stage and ends with reckoning of a whole life; Ecclesiastes tells the young person to rejoice while young but to know God will bring these acts into judgment.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: decreeing justice
row.note: The package's root table offers an unverified sound correspondence; Wisdom says rulers decree justice by her, linking the commentary's counsel in haqq to enacted right order rather than merely to a seasonal due date.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: annual perpetual ordinance
row.note: The table offers an unverified sound correspondence; the exodus day is to be remembered as a festival through generations by perpetual חקה, making a fixed calendar date bind successive people.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: day-night covenant at its time
row.note: The table's proposed sound correspondence is unverified; Jeremiah says the covenant with day and night would have to be broken for either to fail to come at its appointed time, tying the commentary's sequence to reliable recurrence.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: unjust decrees
row.note: The table offers only a sound correspondence; Isaiah denounces those who inscribe unjust decrees, showing that a prescribed order can oppose the commentary's haqq and righteous action when its content is corrupt.

row.basis: Gathered festivals rejected without justice
row.note: The commentary says a community persists through righteous conduct, truth, and patience; Amos has God reject its festivals and solemn assemblies, complicating the assumption that recurring gatherings alone preserve a people.

row.basis: Justice must flow continually
row.note: The commentary joins truthful counsel to the group's endurance; after rejecting festivals Amos calls for justice to roll like water and righteousness like an enduring stream, identifying the needed practice beyond assembly.

row.basis: One hour of repentance and good deeds
row.note: The commentary says long earthly time contracts to an hour and makes righteous action decisive; Avot values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world while separately valuing an hour of the coming world's peace.

row.basis: If the dead do not rise, eat and drink
row.note: The commentary reports deniers who treat mortal time as final; Paul voices the practical conclusion of denying resurrection, eating and drinking because tomorrow brings death, then challenges that premise in his resurrection argument.

row.basis: The dead rise according to deeds
row.note: The commentary's final compressed stay ends in loss for deniers and survival through right action; Jesus says those in the tombs come out to resurrection of life or judgment according to what they have done.

row.basis: The dead judged from records of deeds
row.note: The commentary reports that time itself is said to destroy and recalls an accounting after a brief-seeming stay; Revelation has the dead stand before the throne as books are opened and each is judged by deeds.

row.basis: Merchants plan a profitable year
row.note: The commentary recalls competitive accumulation that hides life's shortness; James addresses people planning a year of travel and trade for gain, the precise plan exposed as uncertain in the next verse.

row.basis: Self-stored goods versus wealth toward God
row.note: The commentary opposes multiplication of possessions to deeds that endure; Jesus closes the rich fool's story by contrasting storing up for oneself with being rich toward God.

row.basis: Delay produces sleep in a waiting group
row.note: The commentary gives broken sleep a place between periods of waiting; in Jesus' bridegroom story the delay makes all the attendants drowsy and asleep before the decisive arrival.

row.basis: Prepared attendants enter before the door closes
row.note: The commentary asks who remains when an apparently long wait abruptly ends; in the bridegroom story those prepared enter the feast on his arrival and the door is shut.

row.basis: Times and seasons introduce the final Day
row.note: The commentary moves from named periods to a sudden terminal hour; Paul explicitly invokes times and seasons before describing the Lord's Day as unexpectedly arriving in the following verse.

row.basis: Steadfastness joined to enduring work
row.note: The commentary's remaining group combines persistence with righteous deeds; Paul concludes his resurrection argument by telling believers to be steadfast and always active in the Lord's work because that labor is not futile.

row.basis: Human flesh as grass
row.note: The commentary reduces a human lifetime to a passing interval; Peter applies Isaiah's fading-grass image to all flesh, making mortal brevity part of his appeal to a community born through the gospel.

row.basis: Enduring word against passing life
row.note: The commentary joins short human life to truth that can hold people together; Peter completes the Isaiah citation by contrasting fading humanity with the Lord's enduring word and identifies that word with what was proclaimed to his hearers.

row.basis: A new Today after a long time
row.note: The commentary describes time as linked parts in which an appeal remains open; Hebrews says God appoints another day called Today after a long time, using David's warning to demand a present response.

row.basis: Now is the accepted time and day of rescue
row.note: The commentary's finite interval calls for righteous response before the end; Paul applies a promise about the favorable time and salvation day to his hearers' present now.

row.basis: Keep watch because the hour is unknown
row.note: The commentary stretches patience through uncertain time before the final contraction; the Didache tells believers to watch their lives and keep lamps ready since they do not know the Lord's hour.

row.basis: Meet often; faith must endure to the end
row.note: The commentary connects repeated meetings among people with the need to remain through time; the Didache urges frequent gathering for the soul and says a lifetime of faith is of no benefit unless completed at the end.

row.basis: Lights govern day and night and distinguish them
row.note: The commentary holds night and day together without dissolving their distinction; Genesis says the lights govern the two periods and separate light from darkness, adding ordered difference to their succession.

row.basis: Sun governs the day
row.note: The commentary's two daily periods are each assigned a place; the litany names the sun as ruler of the day, with its companion night assignment in the next verse.

row.basis: Moon and stars govern the night
row.note: The commentary pairs night with day as adjacent ordered parts; the litany gives the night to moon and stars after naming the sun's daily rule in the preceding verse.

row.basis: Horn blown at recurring lunar feast
row.note: The commentary extends morning-evening segments to prescribed seasonal observance; the psalm orders the horn at new moon and full moon for the festival day, whose status as statute is given in the next verse.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: festival statute
row.note: The root table supplies an unverified sound correspondence; the festival marked in the preceding verse is called a חק for Israel, connecting a recurring appointed day to a shared obligation.

row.basis: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew חקק: enduring cosmic decree
row.note: The table's sound correspondence is unverified; God establishes the heavenly bodies permanently and gives them a decree that will not pass, an ordinance behind the commentary's dependable recurring periods.

row.basis: Mortal grass fades while divine word stands
row.note: The commentary joins a vanishing human lifespan to the truth that sustains the community; Isaiah says the grass withers and flower fades but God's word remains forever.

row.basis: Acceptable fasting frees the oppressed
row.note: The commentary ties calendrical practice to righteous action; Isaiah defines God's chosen fast as releasing unjust bonds and freeing the oppressed, giving a concrete ethical test for a designated day.

row.basis: Humans do not know their fatal time
row.note: The commentary says a long life can suddenly end in a fraction of a day; Ecclesiastes says people do not know their time and compares their capture by disaster to fish and birds trapped unexpectedly.

row.basis: Nighttime recitation has a bounded interval
row.note: The commentary makes night a distinct period filled with a sustained religious act; the Mishnah asks when the evening Shema is read and sets competing limits within the night's watches.

row.basis: Morning recitation begins with visible dawn
row.note: The commentary joins morning to the night before it as a new part of disciplined time; the Mishnah asks when morning Shema begins and uses the ability to distinguish colors to mark the transition.

row.basis: Fixed instruction must become deeds
row.note: The commentary couples counsel in truth with righteous works; Shammai says to make Torah study regular, speak little, and do much, specifying how words and acts should be ordered across ordinary time.

row.basis: Continue the work though it cannot be finished
row.note: The commentary's patient group persists across a life too short to encompass everything; Avot says one need not finish the work but is not free to abandon it.

row.basis: Prepare in this life's antechamber
row.note: The commentary treats mortal time as a bounded span before the final meeting; Avot likens this world to an antechamber where one prepares before entering the coming world's hall.

row.basis: Righteous souls ask how long they must wait
row.note: The commentary links patient waiting to the final reckoning; the souls of the righteous ask from their chambers when the reward will arrive, making the interval after death itself a question. Numbering of 4 Ezra varies by edition.

row.basis: Waiting ends when the number is complete
row.note: The commentary says people remain linked through a long interval before its end; the angel's reply makes the completion of the number of the righteous the limit of their wait. Numbering of 4 Ezra varies by edition.

row.basis: The present form of the world is passing
row.note: The commentary says a seemingly stable span is already vanishing; Paul tells those engaged with the world not to live as though its present form were lasting.

row.basis: Servants wait to admit the returning master
row.note: The commentary links people through patient readiness during uncertain time; Jesus compares disciples to servants waiting for their master so they can open immediately when he arrives.

row.basis: Unknown day and hour demand watchfulness
row.note: The commentary compresses the end of a long interval into an unexpected moment; the bridegroom parable concludes with an instruction to stay awake because the day and hour are unknown.

row.basis: Night-and-day prayer seeks to strengthen others
row.note: The commentary makes mutual support stretch through both parts of the day; Paul describes earnest night-and-day prayer to see his hearers again and supply what their faith lacks.

row.basis: Night-and-day labor spares the community
row.note: The commentary connects righteous work across the daily cycle with people sustaining one another; Paul says his group worked night and day so they would burden none of the believers.

row.basis: An aged witness awaits a promise before death
row.note: The commentary sets divine promise within the finite span of a life; Simeon has been told he will not see death before seeing the Messiah, making his later waiting answer a personal life limit.

row.basis: One hour compared with the whole day's labor
row.note: The commentary compresses a long stay to an hour and asks what deeds count at its end; the first workers complain that those hired last worked only one hour yet received an equal wage, a parabolic comparison rather than a statement that all lives are equally long.

row.basis: Past, present, and future held in the mind
row.note: The commentary argues that lived time consists of joined pieces rather than a single flat flow; Augustine describes a present of remembered past, attended present, and expected future, offering a later Christian account of how those parts are connected.

row.basis: Good not withheld from upright walkers
row.note: The commentary makes righteous conduct the condition of continuing good through time; the psalm says God withholds no good from those who walk uprightly. The verb uses Hebrew עצר, the package's sound correspondence to Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r, but restraint here has no established cognate link to the commentary's time sense.

row.basis: The impious call life short and death final
row.note: The commentary reports those who think time alone destroys them; Wisdom assigns to its impious speakers the claim that life is short and no remedy follows death, but the book frames their reasoning as unsound.
